idiom_name: record version chain (readonly record + with expression) over an ordered history list
implementation_notes: C# records cover the Version role: positional records are init-only and a with expression performs the non-destructive mutation, so publishing a version is Current with { Fee = 12.5m } appended together with its DateTimeOffset effective date - no hand-written copy method. The continuity is an ordinary class owning the ordered history; as-of reads use FindLastIndex for short histories or List.BinarySearch over a maintained date list when history is long. The classic two-class structure survives only where a version must be a mutable entity for the ORM; when the model is persisted, EF Core's SQL Server temporal tables (second variant) let the database own the history instead.
pitfalls: A with expression copies references: a record member that is a List or Dictionary is shared with the previous version, so one in-place edit rewrites history - copy nested collections or make the members immutable.

DateTimeOffset comparisons are instants while DateTime comparisons depend on Kind (Unspecified compares as local time); mixing them, or persisting local time into a UTC temporal column, shifts effective dates.
List<T>.BinarySearch requires the list to be sorted by the searched key or the result is simply incorrect; use a date-only comparer over a maintained sorted list, or FindLastIndex.

An ORM entity used as the version type acquires identity and change tracking, so a tracked 'old' version can be saved over the current one - keep versions immutable records and never let SaveChanges see them as modified.

variants.name: SQL Server system-versioned temporal tables through EF Core
variants.idiom_name: EF Core TemporalAsOf / TemporalAll over system-versioned tables
variants.implementation_notes: With EF Core on SQL Server the version role moves into the database: the entity maps to a temporal table (period columns ValidFrom/ValidTo plus a history table) and the continuity is the entity key, while the query operators TemporalAsOf, TemporalAll, TemporalFromTo, TemporalBetween and TemporalContainedIn translate to FOR SYSTEM_TIME ... AS OF - so 'the contract as of 1 March' is a LINQ call instead of a hand-maintained version list. Historical queries are always no-tracking and read the history table, and system versioning records record time (what the row looked like at each commit), which is not the same as a business effective date: a retroactive amendment still needs its own effective-date column. Keep the as-of method in the domain so callers never see the persistence detail.
pitfalls: System versioning is record time, not effective time: an amendment committed today appears as of today, so effective-date semantics still need their own version rows or columns.
Temporal queries are always no-tracking and return detached copies, so change tracking, lazy loading and updates against them behave differently from ordinary queries.
The history table grows with every update and is part of the schema; retention, period-column hiding and indexes on ValidFrom/ValidTo must be planned.
Arguments are interpreted as UTC: passing local DateTime values to TemporalAsOf gives unexpected results near midnight and across zones.
